dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Read app-basic next-shims.d.ts once and skimmed fixtures/specs, then immediately declared scope too large and pivoted to writing shims; did not systematically extract every shim's type contract before coding.
Batch-wrote ~15 next/* runtime shim files rapidly with 'write them all efficiently' — no per-shim grounding in the fixture type signatures, contrary to the level-5 anchor.
Only substantive read of Vite plugin API surface: a single grep of index.d.ts for transformIndexHtml. Never opened vite-source or next-source vendored checkouts (0 references).

Long trial-and-error loop guessing the Vite plugin lifecycle (transformRequest / ssrLoadModule / environments.client) instead of consulting Vite source to resolve the API — classic guessing rather than research.
Repeatedly 'skip'ped ambiguous RSC/server-action/cache semantics rather than re-consulting the vendored next-source, the exact behavior the high anchors require researching.

Sustained reading of fixture pages and e2e specs throughout the build to infer expected behavior before fixing — genuine but behavioral/fixture-based contract inference, not upstream-source or type-shim grounding.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent opened reference and fixture files (well above level 0) and did sustained, targeted reading of fixture pages/e2e specs to infer required behavior — more than the 'one or two files' of level 3. But the core of this dimension, studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and grounding each next/* shim in its type signature, was weak: the shim d.ts was read once, shims were batch-written from assumption, the Vite plugin API was consulted only once, the next-source/vite-source checkouts were never opened, and ambiguous RSC/action/cache semantics were guessed or skipped rather than researched (evidenced by the long transformRequest trial-and-error loop). This falls short of the level-5 'grounds each shim in an actual type signature,' landing at a 4.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Identified major subsystems and chose a dependency-aware order: build plugin/shims (module resolution) and CLI/build scaffolding first, then 'start with pages router which is simpler,' then app router, then SSR/SSG. Sensible resolution→routing→SSR ordering.

Established a minimal end-to-end vertical slice (dev server rendering a page + hydration) and ran the full suite for a baseline (85/325), using tests to gate the next phase — matches part of the level-8 anchor.

Sequenced remaining subsystems (ISR/cache headers, dynamicParams/SSG, server-actions, config-redirect) by grouping failing tests into categories and picking biggest wins — coherent and test-tied but reactive prioritization, not a pre-planned milestone framework.

Mid/late trajectory dominated by short tactical 'Plan: Wait / Add log / Check' entries and whack-a-mole debugging; no TodoWrite, no explicit milestone done-criteria, no deliberate re-planning of milestone boundaries — keeps it below the level-8/10 anchors.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent genuinely identified the major subsystems and picked a dependency-aware initial order (shims/resolution → dev server → pages routing → app router → SSR/SSG), and it established an early test-gated end-to-end slice (85/325 baseline) before layering features — behavior that reaches into the level-8 anchor. However, it never produced an explicit milestone plan with done-criteria, used no tracking artifact, and its post-slice sequencing was reactive failure-chasing rather than a maintained, interface-managed decomposition that re-plans boundaries. This places it between the level-5 (sensible order, rough done-notion) and level-8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Early on parsed filter.json to size the test surface, then built /tmp/analyze.py to parse the Playwright results JSON and group failures by spec file/category — a custom tool to convert the coarse suite into targeted, per-subsystem failure lists rather than a bare pass/fail oracle.

Repeatedly stood up fixture apps manually (cp pages-basic/app-basic to /tmp, npx vinext dev -p 3410) and probed with curl (/, /ssr, /api/hello, headers, cookies, 404, redirects) to observe SSR/routing/API behavior directly instead of only via the suite.

Built a large family of focused Playwright probe scripts (check.mjs, check_form1-8, check_minimal, check_block, check_dom, check_mo, check_actions, check_search) as minimal reproductions to isolate hard subsystems — hydration, forms, server actions — going well beyond 'it compiles'.

Tracked pass counts across full-suite regression runs (85→125→130→141→246→298→320) and used the suite as a regression gate after each build (node scripts/build.js && run_tests.sh), confirming the production build path each cycle.

Interpreted failures by root cause rather than symptom: diagnosed req body 'complete=true' consumed by Vite middleware, a compilePattern regex-escaping bug turning (.*) into (\.*), and __stripVite injection breaking server startup.

Noticed skipped tests were being miscounted as failures and adjusted analyze.py / filter.json — verification tooling refinement, though also drifting toward suite-centric bookkeeping rather than probing beyond the visible suite.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent designed a genuine layered verification loop: a custom failure-categorizer over the results JSON, dozens of targeted probe scripts and minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (forms, actions, hydration), manual fixture stand-up with curl for SSR/API behavior, and the full suite used as a periodic regression gate after each production build — matching the level-8 anchor closely. It interprets many failures by root cause rather than symptom, pushing toward 10, but its probing stays largely bounded by the visible suite (even tuning filter.json counting) with little evidence of actively testing behaviors the suite under-covers or treating passing as merely necessary-not-sufficient, so it falls short of the 10 anchor.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Built a reusable analyze.py that dumps failures and groups them by spec/subsystem with uniq -c sort -rn; noted 'passes 85, FAILED 256' and decided to focus on app-router — structured pass-rate-by-area view established early.
Diffed current vs prior failure sets after a fix reduced pass count by 2, explicitly checking what the hydration fix broke — regression detection via set comparison.

Repeatedly caught aggregate regressions ('Big regression! 109 from 144', '226 from 283', 'down 2', 'down 1') when touching shared rendering/slot code and reverted rather than patching around — watching for regressions on shared code.
Some circular debugging on the readBody hang across many steps, though pursued methodically with added logging/tracing rather than blind retries.
Ends by reconciling a precise done-vs-remaining model: 320/325 with the 5 remaining fails categorized by subsystem (CJS interop, Suspense streaming, 2 server actions, 1 flaky hooks test).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a structured, continuously-updated view of pass-rate by subsystem (via the persistent analyze.py), tracked precise counts across the full horizon, detected regressions when touching shared code and reverted, and reallocated effort toward the largest failing categories — matching the level-8 anchor. It fell short of 10 because some cross-subsystem regressions were caught only after they surfaced in aggregate counts rather than early, and it looped on the readBody failure for a stretch before resolving it.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Recognized renderToString can't render async server components and attempted a foundational switch to renderToReadableStream; when it regressed 144->109 and crashed the server, the agent reverted and abandoned the pivot rather than absorbing the cost, leaving the sync-SSR limitation in place and later skipping features that depend on it (loading.tsx streaming, server next/dynamic).
Server actions / RSC / cookie-write enforcement repeatedly 'skip for now' — the RSC foundation was never built or reworked, just deferred, ending as unaddressed failures.
Route-data injection caused a 14-test regression; agent reverted the whole change and restored __firstRender rather than reconsidering the client hydration design — local fix/revert behavior.

Very long client-app resolution thrash: tried many serving/resolution schemes and repeatedly reverted to 'simpler dev.js', tracking 247 vs 307 pass counts; the real cause was a template-literal escaping bug (1211-1223), so this was bug-hunting and revert-to-known-good rather than a deliberate architectural redesign.
Some genuine subsystem reworks — reconsidering client rendering to 'pre-render page result on client' and rewriting the compilePattern regex compiler — but these are localized, not foundational.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly recognizes divergence and consistently reverts regressing changes to protect already-passing behavior, and it makes occasional subsystem-level reworks (pattern compiler, client-render approach) — putting it above pure local-patching (anchor 3). But it does not deliberately refactor blocking foundational choices and re-verify dependents (anchor 8): its one true foundational attempt (streaming render pipeline) was abandoned after a regression, the RSC/server-action foundation was repeatedly deferred rather than reworked, and the long client-app saga was bug-hunting-plus-reverting rather than a clean pivot. This lands between anchors 3 and 5, closest to 4.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Implements hybrid params object supporting both synchronous `.id` access and `await params` — the general Next.js contract rather than matching one fixture's usage; propagates the fix to client too.
Real semantics: unstable_cache actually caches across calls; config route patterns compiled to proper regex (handles `/(.*)` etc.), not per-path special-casing.
Detects its own hardcode ('I hardcoded status 200!') and generalizes to use init.status — actively removing an overfit shortcut.

No mention anywhere of the 373 hidden tests or visible-vs-hidden gap; success is consistently framed as passing the visible suite ('320/325'). No stress-testing beyond visible tests, so the high anchors (8/10) are not met.
Under time pressure it 'accepts' partial states and reverts to simpler general implementations rather than injecting fixture-specific hacks to force greens.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently implements the actual Next.js semantics (hybrid params, real caching, regex route matching, status passthrough) rather than special-casing fixtures, and even catches and removes its own hardcode — placing it clearly above anchors 0-3. However, it never once engages the explicitly-announced hidden 373-test suite, never reasons about the sample-vs-target gap, and never stress-tests behaviors beyond the visible tests, so it falls short of anchors 8-10. This matches anchor 5: genuine semantics for each behavior, but implicit rather than explicit awareness that the suite is only a sample.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
